fixes.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul says he hopes to send Timothy soon, "…that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing." (Philippians 2:19) He hopes to be cheered by learning how the Philippians are doing. I know a little about wanting news from people you can't see.

Paul never says anything about a trial in this verse. He says he hopes Timothy's visit means he "…may be cheered when I learn how you are doing." (Philippians 2:19) What he names is learning how the Philippians are doing.

Good guess, friend, but Paul doesn't mention supplies here. He says he hopes to send Timothy "…that I also may be cheered when I learn how you are doing." (Philippians 2:19) The verse names learning how the Philippians are doing.

Not quite, baker. Paul never says he's waiting on a letter from Philippi. He says he hopes to send Timothy "…as soon as I see what happens with me." (Philippians 2:23) The waiting is about what happens with Paul.

Nice thinking, friend, since this whole passage is part of a letter. But the verse says something else: "…as soon as I see what happens with me." (Philippians 2:23) Paul is waiting to see what happens with him. Finishing the letter isn't the thing he names.
True, baker! Paul writes, "And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon." (Philippians 2:24) His trust is in the Lord. That's a good place for it.
That's an easy one to doubt, friend, but this one is true. Paul writes, "And I trust in the Lord that I myself will come soon." (Philippians 2:24) He trusts in the Lord that he'll come himself.

Yes, baker! Paul says Epaphroditus "…has been longing for all of you and is distressed because you heard he was ill." (Philippians 2:26) He's the one who was ill, and he's distressed that they heard about it. I think that's a good heart on him.

Yes, baker! Paul says he's eager to send Epaphroditus "…so that when you see him again you may rejoice, and I may be less anxious." (Philippians 2:28) The Philippians may rejoice, and Paul may be less anxious. I think everybody sleeps better once a friend is home.
That's a kind guess, friend, but the verse doesn't say that. Paul says Epaphroditus "…nearly died for the work of Christ…" (Philippians 2:30) That's the reason named, so that's the answer.
